items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes (DB's Mallika Sachdeva)
items.title: Semis trade just passed oil & gas: the first time in modern history. Welcome to the chip-dollar
items.idea: Deutsche Bank's Sachdeva: four-quarter global semiconductor exports through Q2 2026 exceeded oil and gas trade for the first time in modern history. Her thesis is that Asian tech-export surpluses now recycle into US assets (mostly US tech equity) the way petrodollars recycled into Treasuries. That props up dollar dominance but adds a new source of instability: the recycling channel is now tied to AI equity sentiment rather than oil prices.
items.angle: Petrodollars bought Treasuries. Chip-dollars buy $NVDA and $MSFT. So an AI equity drawdown is now also a dollar-flow event, which helps explain why DXY and the AI trade have been moving together. Japan's record October exports (chip-led, per Mando) are the same story.
items.tweetA: For 50 years the dollar's plumbing ran through oil. As of Q2 2026, global chip exports are bigger than oil and gas exports. The petrodollar recycled into Treasuries. The chip-dollar recycles into the Nasdaq. Ask yourself what a 35% drawdown in $NVDA does to that loop.
items.tweetB: The new dollar risk isn't OPEC. It's Taiwan, Korea and Japan deciding US tech is too expensive to keep recycling their surpluses into. Korea and Taiwan equities are already cracking (Taiwan needed a short-selling ban). Watch $KRW and $TWD as the dollar's new tell.

charts.desc: Global semiconductor exports vs oil & gas exports (4Q sum): chips cross above energy for the first time. Charts inside, worth opening

items.title: 'Sentiment is washed out'? Record household equity allocation and record leveraged-ETF dip buyers say otherwise
items.idea: MacroEdge rejects the 'washed out' narrative on X: household allocation to equities is at an all-time high, daily dip buyers in leveraged ETFs are at a record, and retail futures-leverage products (now including Robinhood) are being rolled out en masse. They call 2023-2026 'Powell's Valhalla', a regime that bred a once-in-a-lifetime buy-the-dip crowd that will ignore the obvious warning signs.
items.angle: Survey sentiment (put/call 3rd-highest in a year, BofA funds cutting tech) can be bearish while household stock positioning stays near max long. Retail and institutions are positioned in opposite directions, so a bounce gets sold by institutions and a breakdown lands on retail.
items.tweetA: Put/call ratios say fear. Household equity allocation says all-time high. Both are true: institutions are hedged, retail is levered. Washed-out markets don't have record leveraged-ETF dip buying.
items.tweetB: Every cycle the gambling products show up last. This month retail got more ways to lever up on futures, and that's the late-cycle tell. The product pipeline is a better sentiment indicator than any survey.

charts.desc: Dow Jones daily: uptrend from 4/25 under threat; tech index chart with no lower low yet. Charts inside, worth opening

items.title: Oil and equities fell, but 2s and 10s didn't move. The inflation isn't coming from energy
items.idea: MacroEdge: with the December hike priced at 100% under the Warsh Fed, 2-year and 10-year yields have not declined while oil and equity indices both dropped. Their read is that much of the recent inflation input hasn't been energy costs. Oil is now trading with the Nasdaq on growth fears.
items.angle: This fits Noahpinion's 'broad-based' CPI chart and the Citadel Securities chart showing the share of CPI components running above 3%. If yields hold while oil falls, the bond market is pricing sticky core inflation, and duration doesn't hedge an equity drawdown in this regime.
items.tweetA: WTI is down from $106 to $85 and the 10-year won't budge. That tells you what the bond market thinks is driving inflation, and it isn't oil. Duration isn't your hedge this cycle. $TLT
items.tweetB: The cleanest macro signal this week isn't Nvidia. Oil and stocks both fell and yields held flat. When the curve ignores a falling oil price, the Fed has a services problem, not an energy problem.

items.title: Taiwan had to 'effectively ban' short selling to stop the bleed. Korea got no reprieve
items.idea: MacroEdge notes South Korea saw 'little reprieve' and Taiwan was briefly saved by an effective ban on short selling, while charts of SPY, DIA and IWM are converging into similar patterns, which they say typically happens at major turning points.
items.angle: Short-sale bans are policy signals of stress. They also mark the chip-export economies that are the source of the new 'chip-dollar' recycling flows (DB/Sachdeva). Asian authorities are defending the AI-supply-chain equity complex.
items.tweetA: Taiwan banning short sales to protect the AI supply chain trade is not a bullish data point. It's the same playbook as Korea 2020 and China 2015. Bans delay price discovery. They don't change it.
items.tweetB: Track this: the economies that print the chip surplus are now intervening in their own equity markets. If chip-export capital stops recycling into the US, the effect shows up in FX before it shows up in $SOXX.

items.title: Hormuz flows are down for two weeks, yet WTI fell from $106 to the $80s. Freight stopped passing through
items.idea: Iran has re-escalated in the Strait of Hormuz with drone and missile strikes on several countries, and flows have 'dipped noticeably' over two weeks. But WTI fell from a late-October high of ~$106 because freight-rate declines are no longer passed through to the barrel, and US/EU growth fears dominate. MacroEdge warns a cycle high in WTI is still possible in 2027.
items.angle: Oil is now a growth asset trading with the Nasdaq, so supply risk is underpriced while the AI trade drags crude. FX Daily (Innes) flags the same tail: an Iranian oil spike puts a 50bp Fed hike back on the table.
items.tweetA: Hormuz flows are falling and Iran is firing drones again, yet oil is down 20% because it trades like a tech stock now. When the Nasdaq stops driving crude, supply will matter again in a hurry. $USO $XLE
items.tweetB: The Jensen saga pulled every eyeball away from the Gulf. That's when supply shocks get mispriced. Lower Hormuz flows, more US carriers heading in, and WTI at $85. Cheap convexity.

items.title: Post-Jensen Nvidia = 'middle-management mindset'. And the Anthropic IPO lands on top
items.idea: MacroEdge calls NVDA's print 'plain vanilla' and expects growth to slow 'rather dramatically' as middle-management mindsets replace an innovator at the top. They expect the Anthropic IPO on Thursday to bring short-term 'TACO' support from the administration, and liken a subsequent OpenAI IPO to 'dropping yet another boulder on top of a sandcastle'.
items.angle: The supply side of the AI trade is the risk: Anthropic, then OpenAI, then SpaceX's chip financing all compete for the same AI capital pool. Equity supply has to be absorbed just as the incumbent leader loses its founder.
items.tweetA: Two mega AI IPOs in a row is a supply event, not a sentiment event. Every dollar that goes into $ANT at IPO is a dollar that doesn't go into $NVDA at 35% off its high.
items.tweetB: Founder-led to committee-led is the most underpriced transition in tech. Apple post-Jobs kept compounding on the existing product line for a decade, but it stopped making new category bets. Nvidia's next decade depends on new category bets.

items.title: Dow's uptrend from April is under threat, and SPY/DIA/IWM charts all look the same
items.idea: MacroEdge: the false breakout a few weeks ago was 'brutally faded'. A breakdown in the Dow's uptrend from 4/25 would validate their 'revenge of the old world' thesis. But no lower low in tech yet means it's 'not time to press the short side', and the next 8-16 weeks decide direction.
items.angle: A disciplined 'wait for confirmation' stance from a bear is notable. Pair it with Rosenberg's 7,002-6,920 S&P fourth-wave support to get concrete levels for the breakdown trigger.
items.tweetA: Even the bears are saying: don't press shorts until tech prints a lower low. That's the tell that this is a 'breakdown pending' market, not a crash. Define your trigger level and wait.
items.tweetB: When SPY, DIA and IWM all draw the same chart, correlation has gone to one. That's the opposite of what you'd see in a healthy rotation.

items.title: Startup grants priced by expected value: the Tony Elumelu prize is worth $60 per application
items.idea: Of 454 non-dilutive programmes, only 15 publish success rates. Expected value per application: Tony Elumelu Foundation $5k at 1.2% odds (265k applicants) = $60. Innovate UK Women in Innovation ≈ $3.4k. DoD SBIR Phase I ≈ $30k (funding rate fell from 20.5% in FY19 to 12.1% in FY23). Eurostars 19.1% ≈ $80k. EIC Accelerator 8.6% on a ~€2.4M grant ≈ $236k. A UK ERIS R&D tax claim on $400k of spend returns ~$108k at 100% odds.
items.angle: Non-dilutive capital is shifting from competitions to tax plumbing, which favours founders with good accountants over founders with good essays. DoD SBIR Phase I odds falling while defense-tech VC booms means the government is rationing at the bottom of the funnel.
items.tweetA: A $5,000 startup grant with 265,000 applicants is worth $60 per application, less than the hourly rate of whoever writes it. The UK R&D tax form on $400k of spend is worth $108k at 100% odds. Founders keep buying the lottery ticket and skip the refund.
items.tweetB: DoD SBIR Phase I acceptance fell from 20.5% to 12.1% in four years, while defense-tech VC hit records. Once you're in, Phase II funds 51.7% of proposals. The government is the hardest LP to meet and the easiest one to re-up.

charts.desc: Grant expected value chart (award × published odds) vs ERIS claim; R&D refund by country. Charts inside, worth opening

items.title: Governments quietly switched R&D support from grants to tax: 28% → 60% of support since 2004
items.idea: OECD (June 2026): tax incentives are now ~60% of government support for business R&D, vs 28% in 2004. HMRC is cracking down: claims fell 17% to 40,325, and SME/ERIS relief fell 29% to £2.3B. On the same $400k of R&D, Australia's refundable offset returns $174k and the US payroll offset only $24k. Canada doubled its enhanced SR&ED limit to C$6M (law since March).
items.angle: R&D support is now a tax-competition variable, much like the corporate tax rate. For a startup deciding where to incorporate and run R&D, Australia/Canada vs the US is a 7x cash-refund gap.
items.tweetA: Same $400k of R&D: Australia refunds $174k. The US refunds $24k. Nobody talks about this when they debate why startups incorporate in Delaware but put engineers in Toronto.
items.tweetB: Industrial policy didn't disappear. It moved from grant committees to the tax code, where it's invisible and gets no headlines. 60% of government R&D support is now tax relief, up from 28% in 2004.

items.title: Programmes dying quietly: Innovate UK Smart Grants gone, Germany's ZIM frozen, US SBIR lapsed for 195 days
items.idea: 33 of 454 programmes are closed, paused or on new terms. Innovate UK Smart Grants are gone (the replacement, Velocity, opens autumn 2027 and covers only six sectors). Germany's ZIM has taken no new applications since 7 July. US SBIR lapsed for 195 days before reauthorisation on 13 April. New Zealand abolished Callaghan Innovation. The EU de minimis cap of €300k over three years means five small grants can block a sixth.
items.angle: Fiscal tightening in Europe is showing up in innovation budgets before it shows up in headlines. That ties into DB's 'European fiscal concerns' leg of the bearish trifecta.
items.tweetA: Germany stopped taking applications to its flagship SME innovation programme in July. The UK killed Smart Grants. Europe's fiscal squeeze is already hitting startup funding. Watch where the next cut lands.
items.tweetB: The US let SBIR, its main small-business R&D programme, lapse for 195 days this year. Federal R&D funding now carries shutdown-style risk.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes (FX Daily)
items.title: Market prices 75bp more Fed hikes (to 4.50-4.75%), but Williams is pushing back
items.idea: Rates are pricing three more 25bp hikes, taking fed funds toward 4.50-4.75%, after Waller's hawkish intervention and hot data. NY Fed's Williams argues inflation drivers aren't broadening enough for dramatic action, which makes 25bp on Dec 9 more credible than 50bp. ING's Chris Turner sees DXY testing 104.60. Eurozone October inflation is expected at 4.0% headline / 2.5% core.
items.angle: With three hikes already discounted, good US data stops adding fuel to the dollar, so asymmetry is shifting. And a 4% Eurozone headline print alongside EUR/USD below 1.10 means the ECB is in a bind too.
items.tweetA: Market pricing: 3 more Fed hikes. Williams: 'not broadening enough'. Waller: maybe 50bp. When the Fed's own chair-adjacent voices split this wide, the front end is where the vol is. $TLT $SHY
items.tweetB: Eurozone headline inflation at 4.0% and EUR/USD still breaking lower. Usually high inflation strengthens a currency via hikes. When it doesn't, the market is telling you the ECB can't follow.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes (FX Daily)
items.title: Iron ore and copper roll over: AUD, ZAR and BRL are the weak flank of FX
items.idea: Industrial metals are buckling (iron ore weak, copper rolling over, crude down sharply). That's a second, Fed-independent hit to commodity currencies. Innes argues this is typically the first sign of a slowdown that should favour JPY more aggressively. AUD is especially exposed given China's sluggish demand. BRL also has domestic political noise.
items.angle: This lines up with Druckenmiller being short copper and warning about 2H27. A commodity FX short (AUD/JPY) is the cleanest expression of 'Fed tightening into a commodity slowdown'.
items.tweetA: Druckenmiller is short copper. Innes says iron ore and copper are rolling together. The cleanest trade for 'Fed hikes into a global slowdown' isn't in equities. It's short $AUDJPY.
items.tweetB: A currency can fall even when the dollar stops rising, because its export prices are falling. That's the trap for anyone bottom-fishing AUD and ZAR on 'peak dollar'.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes (FX Daily)
items.title: EUR/USD broke 1.1000 and the options market shrugged: 1m risk reversal only 0.5 vol for puts
items.idea: Spot is below 1.1000, but one-month EUR/USD implied vol barely moved and risk reversals are only ~0.5 percentage points in favour of euro puts. Innes reads this as a market already carrying considerable short-euro exposure: trading below 1.10 is position management rather than fresh bearish conviction. 1.0880 is the next downside reference.
items.angle: A spot break without a vol bid is a crowded-trade signal. Cheap EUR calls are a contrarian hedge if Iran de-escalates or US data softens.
items.tweetA: EUR/USD breaks a big figure and nobody pays up for puts. That's not fear. That's a market that's already short. When spot moves and vol doesn't, fade the move or buy the cheap wing.
items.tweetB: Watch the vol surface, not the spot level. 1m EUR/USD risk reversals at just 0.5 for puts after losing 1.10 says the euro bears have run out of new money.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes (FX Daily)
items.title: Iranian drones vs US forces in Kuwait and more US carriers heading to the Gulf: the oil tail that could make the Fed hike 50bp
items.idea: Reports of renewed Iranian drone activity against US forces in Kuwait, continued exchanges around the Gulf and more American aircraft carriers heading into the region. Innes says a renewed oil spike would feed straight into inflation expectations: DXY 104.60 becomes a 'staging post', EUR/USD heads toward 1.0800, and a bigger Fed move returns. Mando also lists 'US, Iran again trade strikes'.
items.angle: This is the mirror image of MacroEdge's point that oil trades with the Nasdaq now. The market prices oil as a growth asset while the geopolitical tail is getting fatter.
items.tweetA: Iranian drones on US forces in Kuwait. More carriers en route. WTI at $85 and falling. If oil spikes here, the Fed goes 50 in December and the dollar runs. The market is pricing none of that convexity.
items.tweetB: Everyone's watching the Fed for the December hike size. The real swing factor is the Gulf. One tanker incident is the difference between 25bp and 50bp.

items.title: Teen happiness may finally be turning, as teens leave public social platforms
items.idea: The Youth Behavioral Risk Survey shows signs that teen unhappiness has started to reverse after a decade-plus decline. CDC data still shows high teen suicide rates, so it's early. The candidate causes are teens moving away from toxic public platforms (X, Facebook) toward private messaging and passive video (TikTok), and actively trying to cut social media use.
items.angle: If teens are shifting from public social feeds to private chat and passive video, engagement and ad models built on public posting (X, Facebook feed) lose the next generation while closed messaging gains. That's a long-duration signal for attention-economy equities.
items.tweetA: Teens are leaving public social media for group chats and passive video. That's not a moral story. It's an ad-inventory story. Public-feed platforms are losing the 2035 consumer now. $META $SNAP
items.tweetB: The smartphone generation's mental health may be turning, and not because of regulation. Users adapted. Bet on adaptation over bans next time a technology panic comes along.

items.title: Is AI getting less bang for the buck? Capability per research dollar is decelerating smoothly
items.idea: Garicano and Imas argue the late-2025/early-2026 speed-up in AI progress came from accelerating research spending, not AI coding tools. Their data shows a smooth deceleration in capability gained per dollar of R&D. Counterpoint: ECI points may be log-scale like the Richter scale, and economic usefulness may be accelerating as models cross thresholds even if raw capability isn't.
items.angle: This is the core of the AI-capex debate. If capability per dollar is falling, frontier labs need ever-larger budgets. Anthropic's compute costs rising to 58% of revenue (Dark Side/Shah) is what that looks like on an income statement.
items.tweetA: Capability per AI research dollar is falling smoothly. Anthropic's compute cost went from 48% to 58% of revenue in one quarter. Two very different sources, same curve: each step forward costs more.
items.tweetB: The AI bull case doesn't need capability per dollar to rise. It needs usefulness per dollar to rise. OpenRouter token volumes up 35x y/y say usefulness is winning, for now.

charts.desc: Garicano/Imas: AI capability index gain per $ of research spending over time. Charts inside, worth opening

items.title: US inflation is back near 5% and broad-based, and real wages are falling again
items.idea: Smith: recent monthly inflation prints are running around 5% annualized, and the acceleration is broad-based, not just oil from the Iran war. Possible causes: budget deficits, Trump pressure on the Fed, data-center cost pressures. Real wages are falling: 'Americans are getting poorer this year', less than in 2021 but enough to make voters angry.
items.angle: Data-center cost pressure as an inflation channel is the underappreciated link: power, construction labour and electrical equipment. That matches the Citadel chart (share of CPI components >3%) and MacroEdge's 'yields didn't fall with oil'.
items.tweetA: The AI buildout is now an inflation input: power, electricians, transformers, construction. The Fed can't hike its way to more substations. That's why core won't break.
items.tweetB: Falling real wages plus a Fed hiking into an equity correction is a political problem before it's a market problem. 2021 cost Biden. 2026 is costing Trump. Pricing in 2027 fiscal stimulus is reasonable.

charts.desc: Monthly CPI annualized ~5%; broad-based inflation breadth; real wage growth turning negative. Charts inside, worth opening

items.title: Inclusionary zoning cuts new housing by 31.8%, costing ~$800k in excess rents per 'affordable' unit
items.idea: Kouchekinia (2026): in California, where more than a third of localities have inclusionary zoning, the typical ordinance cuts annual new residential construction by 31.8%. It also pushes multifamily projects into lower-rent areas, and costs about $800,000 in 'excess rents' paid by market-rate renters per affordable unit created. Some California cities are now cutting the mandates.
items.angle: Supply-side housing reform is becoming bipartisan. That's bullish for multifamily builders and building-products names in reform jurisdictions, and it matters because housing turnover has been flat for four years (Home Depot).
items.tweetA: California forces developers to build 'affordable' units. Result: 31.8% fewer homes and $800,000 in excess rent per affordable unit. Fewer homes overall is the most expensive way to make housing affordable.
items.tweetB: Builder sentiment is at a 2012 low, mortgages are at 7.35%, and many cities still levy a hidden ~1/3 construction tax via zoning mandates. Housing policy has more upside than the Fed does.

items.title: DeepMind's WeatherNext 2: one GPU, hundreds of global scenarios in under 60 seconds. 'Cloud laws' in action
items.idea: WeatherNext 2 beats the previous state of the art on 99.9% of weather variables across a 15-day window and gives a 24-hour advantage in tropical cyclone tracking. It was trained only on marginals (isolated data points) yet correctly predicts the joint systems. Smith frames this as evidence for 'cloud laws': diffuse causal regularities that AI can exploit but humans can't articulate.
items.angle: Weather forecasting is a direct input to power trading, ag commodities, nat gas and reinsurance. A 24-hour edge on cyclones and heatwaves at GPU cost shifts the edge from those who own supercomputers to those who own models.
items.tweetA: A supercomputer used to take hours for what one GPU now does in under 60 seconds, and more accurately on 99.9% of variables. That cost collapse matters for every nat-gas, power and ag trader. Weather edge just got commoditized. $UNG
items.tweetB: The model was never shown the storm systems, only isolated data points, and it predicted the systems anyway. If this generalizes to biology and markets, the scientific method gets a second gear.

items.title: The first US baby bonus works: +7.5% births, but at $107,000 per extra baby
items.idea: Hartley & Jaros on Michigan's Rx Kids ($7,500 baby bonus, launched in Flint in 2024): 2024 births exceeded a three-year baseline by ~7.5%, implying $107k of spending per induced birth. US TFR is ~1.6 vs 2.0-2.1 replacement (a 25%+ gap). South Korea at 0.8 would need a 150% increase, 20x what Michigan achieved.
items.angle: This puts a price on fertility: ~$107k per marginal birth. At US scale, closing the gap to replacement through cash would cost hundreds of billions per year. Demographic decline is effectively locked in, and labour-scarcity themes (automation, robotics, immigration) are the structural bet.
items.tweetA: Price discovery on fertility: $107,000 per extra baby. Closing the US gap to replacement would cost more than the defense budget. Paying for babies won't fix demographics. Robots will have to. $ROK
items.tweetB: Michigan's baby bonus raised births 7.5%. Korea needs +150%, 20x more. No country can pay its way out of a 0.8 TFR. Plan portfolios around shrinking workforces, not reversing them.

items.title: Both US parties are now tax-cut parties: $2.4T average deficits and a ~$5T Democratic spending wishlist
items.idea: America is on track for a $2.4T average annual deficit over the next decade, and incoming Democrats' agenda (via Eric Levitz) adds nearly $5T of new spending while promising lower inflation and rates and tax hikes only on the very rich. Smith: no exit from the debt problem until a 1992-style fiscal-hawk equilibrium returns.
items.angle: Midterm results now feed into term premium: a Democratic sweep with BBB-scale spending adds to deficits just as the Fed is hiking. That's bearish for the long end and bullish for gold over a multi-year horizon, despite the near-term USD strength.
items.tweetA: Republicans cut taxes. Democrats want to cut taxes for most people AND add $5T in spending. A $2.4T baseline deficit is the floor. Term premium has only one direction to go. $TLT
items.tweetB: 1992: every candidate campaigned on the deficit. 2026: nobody does. Fiscal hawks only come back after the bond market forces them to.

items.source: AI Supremacy / Michael Spencer (guest: Jeff Morhous)
items.title: The personal-agent war: Grok Bot vs OpenAI Dots vs Anthropic Duet vs Meta Muse
items.idea: Persistent personal agents with connected tools and cloud computers that keep working after you close your laptop are now the main consumer AI battleground. Morhous's verdict: Dots if you want one assistant to connect the pieces of your work, Grok Bot (built by the Cursor team at SpaceX's AI unit) if you want explicit workflows around a team of persistent specialists. Anthropic is meanwhile spawning a product universe: Claude Meetings, Whiteboards/Sheets, Personal Finance, Science.
items.angle: The moat is moving from model quality to delegation UX and connectors (email, calendar, docs). The agentic share of tokens at 80% (Nvidia call via Boockvar) shows this isn't niche. It's where the inference demand comes from.
items.tweetA: Nvidia said agentic workloads are 80% of tokens now. The consumer fight over who owns your agent (Dots, Grok Bot, Duet, Muse) is the fight over who owns the inference bill. Distribution beats benchmarks.
items.tweetB: One agent that does everything vs a team of specialist agents. This is the iPhone vs Android debate of the agent era, and it'll decide which lab captures consumer revenue.

items.source: AI Supremacy / Michael Spencer (guest: Jeff Morhous)
items.title: Microsoft, FAA, banks, NSA, Apple iCloud all went down this week, the same week Google declared the era of autonomous AI attacks
items.idea: Spencer lists a cluster of outages (Microsoft, FAA, banks, NSA, Apple iCloud), the same week Google said the era of AI autonomous attacks has arrived, and OpenAI faces lawsuits over its cyber-capable Astra-in-training. He also notes Nvidia did nearly $116B in one quarter, more than Anthropic and OpenAI combined will likely make in a year, and NVDA sits ~36% below its all-time high.
items.angle: Whether or not the outages are linked (Rubio says 'zero evidence'), insurers, CISOs and regulators will price as if they are. Cybersecurity budgets get repriced up, and AI labs face new liability exposure for dual-use cyber models.
items.tweetA: FAA, banks, NSA, Microsoft and Apple all broke in one week. Officials say they're unrelated. Every CISO's 2027 budget meeting will assume they're related. $CRWD $PANW $ZS
items.tweetB: Nvidia booked $116B in one quarter. Anthropic plus OpenAI combined won't make that in a year. The picks-and-shovels seller still out-earns the gold miners. That's still how this boom is built.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes (DB's Henry Allen)
items.title: DB's 'bearish trifecta': Middle East energy shock + AI capex crack + European fiscal stress, and why their interaction isn't a normal risk-off
items.idea: Deutsche Bank's Henry Allen examines three interacting risks: Middle East escalation pushing energy higher, deterioration in the AI investment cycle hitting equities, and renewed European fiscal worries lifting sovereign yields. Key teasers: recovering equities/credit loosen financial conditions in a way that conflicts with monetary policy; the bond market is responding to AI-investment news in ways that change the risk picture; and investors may be underestimating a feature of the current tightening cycle. (Email is a teaser; full piece paywalled.)
items.angle: The key implication: in a hiking cycle, risk-asset rallies are self-defeating, because better financial conditions invite more Fed tightening. That aligns with Shah's point that equity weakness alone won't get a Fed pivot.
items.tweetA: In a hiking cycle, a stock rally is hawkish. Better financial conditions mean more Fed work. That's why every bounce this autumn has faded. DB's trifecta is just the three ways it breaks.
items.tweetB: Oil up, AI down, Bund-OAT spreads wider. Any one is manageable. All three together hit a market that's priced for a soft landing with a hawkish Fed. Hedge the correlation, not the individual risks.

items.title: Macro Charts: 'My ideal scenario is in motion'. Precious metals, Brazil, China, uranium, semis lead. Liquidity and value lag
items.idea: Yesterday's leaders were precious metals, Brazil, China, uranium, semis, biotech and momentum. Factor watch: momentum, growth and quality outperformed while liquidity and value lagged. Macro Charts is making 'KEY portfolio changes, high priority' and following up on sentiment and positioning, saying their ideal scenario is in motion. (Details paywalled.)
items.angle: A sentiment-driven contrarian making high-priority portfolio changes during a capitulation-like week (95% of S&P futures longs underwater per Citi; funds cut tech most since 2006 per BofA) usually means adding risk.
items.tweetA: Momentum and quality led on a day the S&P was below its 200-day. That's not how capitulation usually looks. Leadership survived the drawdown, which is what you'd want to see before a bounce.
items.tweetB: Uranium, semis and China leading together tells you the market thinks the AI-power theme is intact even as NVDA trades 35% below its high.

items.title: State of Onchain Q4/26: 'From slop machines to real businesses serving real needs'
items.idea: 0xJeff summarizes 2024-25 to 2026 as a shift from slop machines to real businesses: bigger addressable markets, better monetization, more investor alignment. The questions moved from 'what's the use case' to 'how much market can you capture, is revenue defensible, how do you accelerate GTM'. Focus has moved from onchain-native to industry institutionalization. (Full narratives and teams paywalled.)
items.angle: This narrative shift (revenue over memes) favours fee-generating protocols like Hyperliquid ($2.52M/day revenue) and stablecoin rails (World Bank, DBS USDC) over L1 beta. That's why BTC can fall to $64k while USDC adoption accelerates.
items.tweetA: Crypto's 2026 story: BTC down 26% in six weeks, yet the World Bank and DBS both plugged into USDC the same day. The token went down. The rails went up. Price your portfolio by revenue, not narrative.
items.tweetB: 'What's the use case?' was the 2021 question. 'Is the revenue defensible?' is the 2026 question. When an industry starts getting asked equity questions, it gets valued like equity. The multiples compress first.

items.title: 'Consumer resilience' didn't exist as a search term until Feb 2025, then peaked in May 2026
items.idea: DiMartino Booth: Google Trends found no measurable searches for 'consumer resilience' in the two decades to 2024. The term appeared in February 2025, peaked in May 2026 and remains at a material level through November. She asks 'which' consumer is being referenced (setting up a K-shaped consumer argument). The word itself comes from Bacon's 1626 experiment on echoes bouncing off surfaces.
items.angle: Buzzwords trend when the underlying fact is in doubt: no one searches 'consumer resilience' when the consumer is fine. That pairs with Noahpinion's falling real wages and Home Depot's -0.5% transactions as a sign the narrative is masking a bifurcation.
items.tweetA: Nobody Googled 'consumer resilience' for 20 years. Then it showed up in 2025 and peaked in May 2026. You only need a word for something once it's in question.
items.tweetB: Retail sales beat, Home Depot big-ticket +4.5%, purchase mortgage apps -18% y/y. That's the K-shape: one consumer buys appliances in cash, the other can't get a mortgage. 'Resilience' describes only one of them.

items.title: Nvidia: cloud industry backlog jumped from $2T to $2.5T in three months
items.idea: From the Nvidia call: 'Cloud industry backlog now sits at $2.5 trillion, up from $2 trillion just three months ago.' Revenue grew 20% sequentially and more than doubled y/y; 'Vera Rubin is off to an extraordinary start'. FY2028 growth outlook raised to ~75% from 70% off a higher base. Board chair Harvey Jones: the board 'does not intend to reinstate Jensen'. A new national security and export control oversight committee was formed.
items.angle: A $500B backlog increase in a quarter is about 4x Nvidia's quarterly revenue. Demand is not the constraint. Financing and power are, which is why Nvidia's tone on vendor financing matters more than the beat.
items.tweetA: Cloud backlog went up $500 billion in three months. That's more than four Nvidia quarters added to the queue in 90 days. The demand-collapse bears have to explain that number. $NVDA $MSFT $AMZN
items.tweetB: $2.5T of cloud backlog against hyperscaler capex of roughly $600-700B a year is 3-4 years of committed work. The constraint is substations, not orders.

items.title: OpenRouter token volume up 35x y/y and 3.5x in three months. Agentic = 80% of tokens
items.idea: Nvidia's call: major frontier labs will contribute ~15% of data-center revenue this year. 'Open models are accelerating': weekly token volume on OpenRouter has surged 35x y/y and 3.5x in just the past three months. Agentic workloads now account for ~80% of tokens.
items.angle: Only 15% of Nvidia's DC revenue comes from frontier labs, so the IPO-driven 'lab bubble' risk is narrower than feared. And 3.5x token growth in a quarter vs B200 rental rates rising (Dark Side/Shah chart) means utilization is tight. Bullish for installed-base owners ($CRWV, hyperscalers).
items.tweetA: OpenRouter tokens: 3.5x in three months. That's a 150x annualized pace. Meanwhile B200 rental prices are rising, not falling. Demand is outrunning supply, and the market is trading NVDA 35% off its high.
items.tweetB: Frontier labs are only 15% of Nvidia's data-center revenue. Everyone's worried about OpenAI and Anthropic financing, but 85% of the demand comes from somewhere else. The concentration risk is smaller than the narrative.

items.title: Nvidia signals a pullback from vendor financing: 'rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments, and guarantees'
items.idea: On the financing commitments that have propped up customers: 'As the market matures and additional sources of capital become available, we are rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments, and guarantees... disciplined in how we commit capital.' This came on the first call without Jensen.
items.angle: This is the most important line for AI credit. If Nvidia steps back as lender of last resort, neoclouds and SPV-financed builds (SpaceX's $40B chip financing, TensorWave's 457MW) need to find third-party capital at higher rates. Watch neocloud HY spreads and GPU-backed ABS.
items.tweetA: Buried in the call: Nvidia is 'rigorously evaluating future commitments and guarantees'. Translation: the vendor-financing backstop for the AI buildout just got a committee. Neocloud credit spreads are the next shoe. $CRWV
items.tweetB: Jensen's Nvidia financed its own customers. Committee Nvidia 'evaluates' guarantees. That's the real cost of the CEO change, and it shows up in credit before earnings.

items.title: Home Depot: housing turnover flat for four years, yet nine straight positive comp quarters from share gain
items.idea: Home Depot: 13 of 16 departments positive. Average ticket +3%, transactions -0.5%. Big-ticket (> $1,000) transactions +4.5% y/y on power and appliances. Pro outperforming DIY. Management: 'housing turnover hasn't moved in four years... 9 positive quarters in a row... This is all coming from share gain.' The stock fell 2.5% on the day.
items.angle: Positive comps entirely from share gain in a market with zero turnover growth is a ceiling, not a trend. When rates eventually fall and turnover unlocks, HD gets operating leverage. Until then, it's a share-gain story vulnerable to Lowe's response.
items.tweetA: Home Depot: 9 straight positive quarters with zero growth in housing turnover. That's pure share-taking. The day mortgage rates break 6%, that comp base gets a second engine. $HD $LOW
items.tweetB: Transactions -0.5%, ticket +3%, big-ticket +4.5%. Fewer people buying more expensive things is the K-shaped consumer in one line.

items.title: 30-year mortgage back to 7.35%: purchase apps -18% y/y, refis -54% y/y

items.angle: With three more Fed hikes priced and 10-year yields not falling even as oil drops, there's no rate relief coming for housing. Builders face sentiment at 2012 lows plus inclusionary-zoning drag (Noahpinion).
items.tweetA: Purchase mortgage apps -18% y/y, refis -54%, builder sentiment at a 2012 low. And the Fed is about to hike three more times. Housing isn't bottoming. It's being suppressed on purpose. $XHB $ITB
items.tweetB: Mortgage rates at 7.35% while the S&P is in a correction. Equities wobble, but the housing market is already in recession by volume.

items.tweetB: OpenAI's GPT-6 Cyber found 35 Apple flaws. An AI found a critical Java bug in software 90% of the F500 runs. The vulnerability backlog is about to grow faster than anyone can patch it. Cyber spend is non-discretionary now.

items.title: SpaceX is leasing $47B of Nvidia chips via $40B of financing, and Nvidia bought 7.7M SpaceX shares in Q3
items.idea: SpaceX is leasing $47B of Nvidia chips, with a $40B chip financing starting this week (Bloomberg). Nvidia bought 7.7M SpaceX shares in Q3. TensorWave signed a 457MW deal with OpenAI. Nvidia boosted its buyback by $150B. SEC is probing whether Nvidia misled investors. Haas and Murphy are named as CEO candidates.
items.angle: The circularity is the story: Nvidia owns SpaceX equity, SpaceX leases Nvidia chips with debt. If Nvidia tightens guarantees (Boockvar), these structures depend on outside lenders. A $40B chip financing is a bellwether deal for GPU-backed credit pricing.
items.tweetA: Nvidia owns SpaceX stock. SpaceX leases $47B of Nvidia chips with $40B of debt. Nvidia buys back $150B of its own stock. Follow the money around the circle and ask who's the actual end buyer.
items.tweetB: The $40B SpaceX chip financing launching this week is the most important credit deal of the quarter. Where it prices tells you what lenders think a GPU is worth in year three.

items.title: Nvidia without Jensen: more conservative on customer financing. Better discipline, less fuel for the buildout
items.idea: Nohshad Shah: Nvidia's engineering, software ecosystem and customer relationships won't vanish, so near-term execution is safe. The risk is that new management becomes more conservative, especially on financing customers, and that conservatism spreads to the uncertain long-term bets founders like Musk and Zuckerberg made before returns were clear. Congressional investigations continue regardless.
items.angle: This independently confirms Boockvar's read of the call language on guarantees. The second-order effect is that neoclouds lose their most patient capital source just as Anthropic's disclosures show how expensive short-term compute is.
items.tweetA: Founders make bets professional managers can't justify to a board. Nvidia just swapped the guy who built CUDA when nobody wanted it for a search committee. The next CUDA bet doesn't get made by committee.
items.tweetB: Conservative Nvidia = less vendor financing = higher cost of capital for every GPU cloud. Jensen's exit is a credit event for neoclouds, not an equity event for Nvidia.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes (Nohshad Shah)
items.title: Data centers: supply +33.7% y/y, vacancy at 1.4%, 80% of construction preleased. Scarcity is winning
items.idea: CBRE H1: primary North American data-center supply up 33.7% y/y, yet vacancy fell to just 1.4%, with 80% of under-construction capacity preleased. 3-10MW rents rose 8.3%. Microsoft attributed its capex shortfall to delayed third-party capacity deliveries, with demand still exceeding supply. Token volumes and B200 GPU rental rates both rose through 2026 (Ramp, Silicon Data, Citadel Securities chart). Shah: 'The premium increasingly belongs to computing capacity capable of earning a return today.'
items.angle: Regulation that slows construction is bullish for installed capacity (DLR, EQIX, hyperscalers). Regulation that slows models is bearish for everyone. Lower capex can mean delivery problems rather than weaker demand, so don't read a capex miss as a demand miss.
items.tweetA: Data-center supply grew 33.7% and vacancy still fell to 1.4%. Rents up 8.3%. And GPU rental rates are rising, not falling. That's the opposite of a glut. $EQIX $DLR
items.tweetB: Microsoft's capex 'miss' was delayed deliveries, not weak demand. A slower buildout is a gift to anyone who already owns powered capacity. Permitting delays are a moat now.

items.title: Anthropic Q3: revenue +47% q/q to $17B, but compute +77%, margin 19%→15%, $901B of commitments
items.idea: Anthropic's updated disclosures: Q3 revenue rose ~47% q/q to $17B. Compute and infrastructure expense rose ~77% to $9.9B, from 48% of revenue to 58%. Adjusted operating margin fell from 19% to 15%, largely from expensive short-term compute. ~$901B of multiyear purchase/lease commitments vs ~$132B of cash. More than 80% of Q3 revenue came from models released in the prior six months. Shah's three hurdles: inference margin, recurring frontier R&D cost, return on committed capital.
items.angle: The '80% of revenue from models under six months old' stat is the key risk: revenue is a treadmill, not an annuity. Any regulatory slowdown in model releases hits revenue directly. With IPO day tomorrow, margin trajectory (compute growing faster than revenue) is the debate.
items.tweetA: Anthropic: $17B quarter, +47% q/q. Compute: +77%. $901B of commitments on $132B of cash, a 6.8x ratio. Growth is extraordinary and so is the leverage to it. $ANT prices tomorrow.
items.tweetB: 80% of Anthropic's Q3 revenue came from models less than six months old. That's not SaaS. It's a fashion house. Every season has to sell, or the revenue disappears. Value it accordingly.

items.title: Q3 productivity +3.6%, ULC -0.7%. That's the only thing standing between the Fed and more hikes
items.idea: Shah: Q3 real GDP +3.4% annualized, private final domestic sales +4.9%, October payrolls +165k with +84k revisions, AHE +0.4% m/m, core CPI +0.3%. Waller said ≥0.3% would warrant considering a 50bp December hike. But Q3 productivity rose 3.6% annualized and unit labour costs fell 0.7%. Financial conditions are still easier than historical average, and equity weakness alone gives limited grounds for relief. A Citadel Securities chart tracks the share of CPI components with >3% annualized inflation.
items.angle: If productivity is the AI dividend, it's disinflationary with a lag. That's the bull case for a 2027 Fed pause. But the Fed needs to see it in services, not just the aggregate. Productivity-led growth with a hawkish Fed is the 1997 setup.
items.tweetA: Private final sales +4.9%. Payrolls +165k with upward revisions. Core +0.3%. And productivity +3.6% with unit labour costs falling. This is either 1997 or 1999, and the Fed thinks it's 1979.
items.tweetB: Productivity +3.6% and unit labour costs -0.7%. If that's AI showing up in the data, the Fed is hiking into a supply-side boom. Historically, that ends in an overshoot and a rapid reversal.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes (Nohshad Shah)
items.title: The regulation framework for AI investors: restrict construction = bullish incumbents. Restrict models = bearish everyone
items.idea: Shah's distinction: political and regulatory restrictions on building new data centers preserve the scarcity value of existing operating capacity. Restrictions on model development or deployment weaken the demand expected to fill it. Shah prefers platforms that monetize deployment across multiple model providers rather than any single frontier lab or infrastructure programme.
items.angle: This is a clean 2x2 for the AI regulatory debate heading into 2027 (Congressional investigations, the Nvidia export committee, state-level data-center moratoria). Own multi-model distribution platforms plus operating capacity. Avoid single-model and unpowered pipeline exposure.
items.tweetA: Every AI regulation headline fits one of two buckets. Restrict building: own existing data centers. Restrict models: own nothing. Know which bucket before you trade the headline.
items.tweetB: The best AI business might not be the best model. It's the toll road that routes demand to whichever model wins this quarter. When 80% of revenue comes from six-month-old models, model risk is a feature you can rent out.

items.title: Nvidia's best quarter ever: $115.8B revenue (+103%), $130B guide with China at zero. Stock +3%
items.idea: Revenue $115.8B (+103% y/y) vs ~$109.1B expected. Data center $107.6B (+110%), now 93% of the company. GAAP net income $65.3B. EPS $2.68 vs $2.47. Q4 guide $130B vs $125.3B consensus, China assumed at zero. But growth decelerates to ~77% ex the extra week, and gross margin guides down ~3 points from 74.8% to 71-72%. Shares ~35% below the October peak near $240. NVDA perps on Hyperliquid did ~$1B/day volume, bouncing off $150 to ~$162.
items.angle: 'The AI business is fine and the AI trade has stopped responding to it.' Slowing growth plus falling margins compresses multiples regardless of size. And NVDA perps trading $1B/day on a crypto venue show where retail leverage on the AI trade now lives.
items.tweetA: $130B Q4 guide with China at ZERO. 74.8% gross margins. The stock moved 3%. When the best print in corporate history gets a shrug, the market isn't pricing this quarter. It's pricing 2028's margin. $NVDA
items.tweetB: Nvidia perps did ~$1B a day on Hyperliquid this week. The marginal price-setter for the world's most important stock might now be offshore crypto leverage. Think about what that does to weekend gap risk.

items.title: 182,000 signed to bring Jensen back, including ~9,000 Nvidia employees. Trump and Musk backed it. The board said no
items.idea: Six days after Jensen Huang resigned from the company he co-founded 33 years ago, he publicly offered to return. Trump and Elon Musk backed it, and a petition passed 182,000 signatures including nearly 9,000 self-identified Nvidia employees. The board unanimously declined. Heidrick & Struggles runs the search; CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO. A National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee is chaired by Suzanne Nora Johnson.
items.angle: A board defying the President, Musk and its own employees only makes sense if the independent investigation's findings are serious. That's a tail risk the 3% bounce doesn't price. The SEC probe (Mando) supports this read.
items.tweetA: A sitting President, the world's richest man and 9,000 of its own employees asked Nvidia's board to bring Jensen back. The board said no, unanimously. Boards don't do that unless they've read something the rest of us haven't.
items.tweetB: Retail investors petitioning to reinstate a CEO is a new cultural phenomenon: founders as political candidates. This is the most visible case yet of 'governance by popularity contest', and it failed.

items.title: GPT-6.2 Astra: 20% price cut to $8/M input, scores 62 vs Claude Fable 5.2's 65, and is OpenAI's first model rated 'High' for AI self-improvement
items.idea: OpenAI released GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol a day before the Anthropic IPO. Astra's input price was cut 20% to $8 per million tokens. It scores 62 on Artificial Analysis's Intelligence Index vs Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 at 65, showed no gain in coding-agent performance, and is OpenAI's first externally released model rated High for AI self-improvement.
items.angle: Timing a price cut and launch 24 hours before a rival's IPO is competitive signalling. A model that trails on intelligence and shows no coding-agent gain, launched with a price cut, suggests price competition is coming to the frontier, which is bad for Anthropic's margin trajectory (already 19%→15%).
items.tweetA: OpenAI drops a model and cuts prices 20% the day before Anthropic's IPO. It still scores 62 vs 65. When the challenger competes on price, the leader's margin is the target. $ANT
items.tweetB: Buried in the release: Astra is the first external OpenAI model rated 'High' for AI self-improvement. That safety tier just went commercial at $8 per million tokens, and nobody's talking about it.

items.title: Anthropic's S-1: Amazon + Alphabet own 28.4% with zero votes. A single Class F share controls 50.1%
items.idea: Per the S-1: Amazon and Alphabet will own a combined 28.4% of Anthropic after its IPO, both in non-voting Class N shares, and a single Class F share held by the founders carries 50.1% of voting power. ANT lists on Nasdaq, trading from Nov 19.
items.angle: This is the most extreme founder-control structure in a mega-cap IPO. It's the exact opposite of Nvidia, where the board just overruled its founder. Index-inclusion rules on dual-class/no-vote shares may cap passive demand, which matters for post-IPO flow math.
items.tweetA: Nvidia's board just overruled its founder. Anthropic's S-1 makes that impossible: one Class F share = 50.1% of the votes. The same week gave us both extremes of founder governance. Which one the market pays up for will tell you a lot.
items.tweetB: Amazon and Google own 28.4% of Anthropic and get zero votes. Hyperscalers are paying for exposure, not control. That's how you finance a lab without it being captured by its cloud provider.

items.title: Druckenmiller is short copper and warns 2H27 'could be economically disappointing'
items.idea: Stanley Druckenmiller says he's short copper and warned the second half of 2027 'could be economically disappointing', citing a Fed that's done cutting, weakening commodities and widening credit spreads. Mando adds that he's flat equities.
items.angle: Druckenmiller short copper plus Innes flagging iron ore/copper rolling over plus DB's AI-capex-crack scenario point the same way. Copper is the cross-asset expression of 'Fed + AI capex slowdown', since grid and data-center copper demand was the bull case.
items.tweetA: Druckenmiller short copper is a short on the AI grid-buildout narrative. If data centers were absorbing all the copper the bulls modelled, he wouldn't be short. One of them is wrong. $FCX $COPX
items.tweetB: Flat equities, short copper, worried about credit spreads. When Druck is defensive on growth while the Fed is still hiking, look at 2H27 cyclicals, not 1H27.

items.title: Glassnode: BTC realized losses vs profits hit levels seen only at the 2018, 2020, 2022 and early-2023 lows
items.idea: Glassnode says Bitcoin's realized losses relative to realized profits have reached levels seen only near the lows of 2018, 2020, 2022 and early 2023. BTC at $64.1k fell from $87k in six weeks, dragged by its correlation to the AI trade. BTC ETFs saw $249M of net outflows Tuesday (ETH ETFs -$29M). ARK sold $84.8M of NVDA the day before earnings and put ~$39.9M into Block, Circle and Coinbase.
items.angle: Capitulation-grade on-chain data plus the 'day 407 of 410' bear-cycle timing (Mando) plus bids stacking below (Glassnode chart) make a credible bottoming setup. The risk is that the AI-trade correlation keeps dragging it lower until the Fed on Dec 9.
items.tweetA: BTC loss realization is at the same level as the lows of 2018, 2020, 2022 and 2023. Four for four, those were great entries. The difference this time is that BTC is trading as a levered AI proxy. $BTC
items.tweetB: ARK sold $85M of NVDA the day before earnings and bought Coinbase, Circle and Block. Cathie is rotating from AI to crypto rails, betting the correlation breaks. Bold.

items.title: Ethereum's Glamsterdam: EIP-8037/8038 could break 10,000-15,000 smart contracts
items.idea: Ethereum developers flagged that two proposed changes in the Glamsterdam upgrade, EIP-8037 and EIP-8038, would raise the gas limit while altering protocol assumptions that an estimated 10,000-15,000 contracts depend on. Separately: Hyperliquid led onchain protocol revenue at $2.52M/day, ahead of Pump.fun ($1.4M) and Polymarket ($595k). MEXC shut its Global Card after its issuer pulled service.
items.angle: Scaling ETH L1 at the cost of breaking backward compatibility is a governance stress test. Meanwhile Hyperliquid out-earning everything (including Polymarket) shows where the fee economy lives: perps on everything, including NVDA.
items.tweetA: Ethereum wants to scale L1. The cost: maybe 10,000-15,000 contracts that assumed the old rules. 'Code is law' meets 'the protocol changed the law'. Watch which DeFi blue chips are on that list. $ETH
items.tweetB: Hyperliquid makes $2.52M a day, nearly 2x Pump.fun and 4x Polymarket. And it's running ~$1B/day of NVDA perps. The best crypto business of 2026 is a stock exchange that never closes.
